slides.display_title: Module 1 Closure and Transition to Leadership Identity
slides.visual_description: Module 1 Closure and Transition to Leadership Identity — Understand the source-grounded summary of Module 1 and the bridge into Module 2, including the shift from innovator mindset to leadership identity.
slides.narration_text: Congratulations—your innovator mindset is now set, and the journey deepens. The main message is simple but consequential: we are crossing from how we think about problems to who we must become to lead change. Treat this as a commitment to identity, not a hunt for more tools. As a closing seam, carry forward the discipline you’ve built here and get ready to shape your leadership stance in the next module.
slides.narrative_arc: From completion of Module 1 mindset work to readiness for Module 2 leadership identity through a forward-looking synthesis and transition.
slides.script_notes: Module 1 Closure and Transition to Leadership Identity — Understand the source-grounded summary of Module 1 and the bridge into Module 2, including the shift from innovator mindset to leadership identity.

slides.visual_description: The Intrapreneurial Mandate in Hospitals — Understand that healthcare innovation in this module is framed as intrapreneurship inside existing hospital systems.
slides.narration_text: Innovation here is an inside game. You are building change within the hospital—working with politics, budgets, and legacy systems rather than routing around them. When you treat constraints as design inputs, you create momentum that can actually survive governance and scale.
slides.narrative_arc: From seeing innovation as a generic idea activity to understanding it as intrapreneurial work inside hospital constraints through explicit framing of politics, budgets, and legacy systems.
slides.script_notes: The Intrapreneurial Mandate in Hospitals — Understand that healthcare innovation in this module is framed as intrapreneurship inside existing hospital systems.

slides.visual_description: Kind vs. Wicked Environments — Understand the distinction between kind clinical environments and wicked healthcare innovation environments.
slides.narration_text: Not all environments reward the same skills. In clinical care, patterns repeat and feedback guides refinement; by contrast, innovation work is ambiguous and the rules keep shifting. Read the environment before you act, or you will apply kind-environment habits to wicked problems and pay for it in rework and resistance.
slides.narrative_arc: From assuming clinical problem-solving and innovation follow the same logic to recognizing innovation as a wicked environment through contrast between repetitive medicine and ambiguous system change.
slides.script_notes: Kind vs. Wicked Environments — Understand the distinction between kind clinical environments and wicked healthcare innovation environments.

slides.visual_description: Why Clinical Medicine Feels Kind — Explain why clinical medicine is described as a kind environment in the source.
slides.narration_text: Clinical medicine feels kind because training maps to recognizable patterns, feedback arrives quickly enough to learn, and the rules of practice are stable. That reliability is why repetition builds mastery—and why those instincts are so strong for you.
slides.narrative_arc: From assuming clinical problem-solving and innovation follow the same logic to recognizing innovation as a wicked environment through contrast between repetitive medicine and ambiguous system change.
slides.script_notes: Why Clinical Medicine Feels Kind — Explain why clinical medicine is described as a kind environment in the source.

slides.visual_description: Why Innovation Work Becomes Wicked — Explain why healthcare innovation is described as wicked, ambiguous, and variable.
slides.narration_text: Innovation work becomes wicked when the goal posts are unclear, feedback is delayed or misleading, and policies or priorities shift mid-journey. That volatility isn’t failure—it’s the terrain. Closing the contrast, hold this thought as we pivot: if the work is wicked, your habits must flex. Next, we’ll make that flexibility concrete.
slides.narrative_arc: From assuming clinical problem-solving and innovation follow the same logic to recognizing innovation as a wicked environment through contrast between repetitive medicine and ambiguous system change.
slides.script_notes: Why Innovation Work Becomes Wicked — Explain why healthcare innovation is described as wicked, ambiguous, and variable.

slides.visual_description: Functional Flexibility — Understand that clinical leaders must adapt beyond rigid specialty tools and borrow from other disciplines.
slides.narration_text: Functional flexibility is your edge in wicked conditions. Borrow frameworks, language, and tools from operations, design, business, and behavioral science when the situation calls for it. Rigid specialty thinking that serves you at the bedside becomes a liability in system change.
slides.narrative_arc: From relying only on specialty-specific habits to embracing cross-functional leadership tools through the expectation of disciplined borrowing.
slides.script_notes: Functional Flexibility — Understand that clinical leaders must adapt beyond rigid specialty tools and borrow from other disciplines.

slides.visual_description: Clinical Diagnosis vs. Systemic Diagnosis — Understand the analogy between clinical diagnosis and operational diagnosis before selecting solutions.
slides.narration_text: Lead innovation with the same diagnostic discipline you trust in clinical care: observe, form hypotheses, confirm, then intervene. One path assesses symptoms to find a cause; the other audits systems to surface a root cause. The shared method is the point—understand before you act.
slides.narrative_arc: From solution-first thinking to disciplined root-cause diagnosis through analogy with clinical diagnostic practice.
slides.script_notes: Clinical Diagnosis vs. Systemic Diagnosis — Understand the analogy between clinical diagnosis and operational diagnosis before selecting solutions.

slides.visual_description: Do Not Prescribe Before Diagnosing — Explain the clinical half of the analogy that anchors the leadership diagnostic mindset.
slides.narration_text: Clinically, you never prescribe before assessing. You gather data, build a differential, and test hypotheses. That same rigor—discipline before remedy—is the anchor for your leadership choices.
slides.narrative_arc: From solution-first thinking to disciplined root-cause diagnosis through analogy with clinical diagnostic practice.
slides.script_notes: Do Not Prescribe Before Diagnosing — Explain the clinical half of the analogy that anchors the leadership diagnostic mindset.

slides.display_title: Do Not Buy or Build Before Diagnosing the Root Cause
slides.visual_description: Do Not Buy or Build Before Diagnosing the Root Cause — Apply the diagnostic analogy to innovation decisions inside operational systems.
slides.narration_text: Operationally, buying or building on first impression is the parallel mistake. The disciplined move is to investigate the system, confirm the root cause, and only then design the solution. Stitching the analogy closed, we’ll now guard against a second trap: falling in love with a solution instead of the problem.
slides.narrative_arc: From solution-first thinking to disciplined root-cause diagnosis through analogy with clinical diagnostic practice.
slides.script_notes: Do Not Buy or Build Before Diagnosing the Root Cause — Apply the diagnostic analogy to innovation decisions inside operational systems.

slides.display_title: Falling in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution
slides.visual_description: Falling in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution — Understand that innovators fail when they become attached to solutions instead of accurately defining the problem.
slides.narration_text: The most common failure in innovation is attachment to a favorite solution before the problem is truly understood. When you’re attached, you reshape the problem to fit your idea. Discipline means staying curious about the problem, especially when that curiosity feels uncomfortable.
slides.narrative_arc: From solution attachment to disciplined problem focus through a direct warning about innovation failure.
slides.script_notes: Falling in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution — Understand that innovators fail when they become attached to solutions instead of accurately defining the problem.

slides.visual_description: Symptom vs. Root Cause — Distinguish between visible pain points and underlying system failure.
slides.narration_text: Visible pain points matter, but they’re rarely the source. Treating symptoms without surfacing underlying causes buys temporary relief and guarantees recurrence. A system that keeps producing the same complaint hasn’t been diagnosed—it’s only been managed.
slides.narrative_arc: From reacting to visible pain to distinguishing hidden system failure through symptom-versus-root-cause analysis.
slides.script_notes: Symptom vs. Root Cause — Distinguish between visible pain points and underlying system failure.

slides.display_title: What Looks Broken vs. What Actually Is Broken
slides.visual_description: What Looks Broken vs. What Actually Is Broken — Explain the operational difference between visible symptoms and underlying causes.
slides.narration_text: What looks broken—complaints, delays, frustration—is the surface presentation. What’s actually broken lives in structure: incentives, accountability, process design. Close the gap by naming the structure, not just the symptom. With that lens in place, we can aim for leverage next.
slides.narrative_arc: From reacting to visible pain to distinguishing hidden system failure through symptom-versus-root-cause analysis.
slides.script_notes: What Looks Broken vs. What Actually Is Broken — Explain the operational difference between visible symptoms and underlying causes.

slides.visual_description: The Lead Domino — Understand that solving the true root cause can eliminate multiple downstream symptoms.
slides.narration_text: Leverage comes from finding the lead domino—the structural fix that, once addressed, collapses a chain of visible failures without separate projects for each symptom. Hunt for the intervention that makes many other problems irrelevant.
slides.narrative_arc: From isolated symptom treatment to leverage-based system change through the idea of the lead domino.
slides.script_notes: The Lead Domino — Understand that solving the true root cause can eliminate multiple downstream symptoms.

slides.visual_description: The 5 Whys Framework — Understand the 5 Whys as the module's primary operational tool for surfacing root causes.
slides.narration_text: Use the Five Whys to move past assumptions and into structure. First, ask why the observed problem happens. Then ask why again, letting each answer become the next question. Keep going until your answer points to something you can actually change.
slides.narrative_arc: From vague operational frustration to a usable root-cause method through repeated why-questioning.
slides.script_notes: The 5 Whys Framework — Understand the 5 Whys as the module's primary operational tool for surfacing root causes.

slides.visual_description: Why the 5 Whys Matters — Explain why the 5 Whys is central to operational diagnosis in this module.
slides.narration_text: Most hospital decisions happen at the symptom level, which is why problems recur. The Five Whys interrupts that cycle—simple, no tech required, and it surfaces what metrics alone miss. It also builds shared understanding by forcing reflection before action.
slides.narrative_arc: From vague operational frustration to a usable root-cause method through repeated why-questioning.
slides.script_notes: Why the 5 Whys Matters — Explain why the 5 Whys is central to operational diagnosis in this module.

slides.display_title: Asking Why Until a Root Cause Emerges
slides.visual_description: Asking Why Until a Root Cause Emerges — Describe the basic action of the 5 Whys framework as stated in the source.
slides.narration_text: State the observed problem clearly—only what you can see and measure. Ask why it’s happening, then ask why again, resisting the urge to stop early. Stop when action becomes possible—when the answer points to something your team can actually change. With that root in hand, we can widen our scan for opportunities.
slides.narrative_arc: From vague operational frustration to a usable root-cause method through repeated why-questioning.
slides.script_notes: Asking Why Until a Root Cause Emerges — Describe the basic action of the 5 Whys framework as stated in the source.

slides.visual_description: The Opportunity Radar — Understand that innovation opportunities are generated by systematically auditing frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
slides.narration_text: Great ideas rarely introduce themselves. Build an opportunity radar by auditing three domains: past frustrations, present workarounds, and future trends. When you scan systematically, you stop waiting for inspiration and start finding leverage.
slides.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
slides.script_notes: The Opportunity Radar — Understand that innovation opportunities are generated by systematically auditing frustrations, workarounds, and trends.

slides.visual_description: Past Frustrations as Opportunity Signals — Identify past frustrations as one source of innovation opportunities.
slides.narration_text: Past frustrations are gold. They mark real pain the system normalized rather than solved. Revisit what was dismissed or tolerated—through an innovator’s lens, those moments often reveal opportunities hiding in plain sight.
slides.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
slides.script_notes: Past Frustrations as Opportunity Signals — Identify past frustrations as one source of innovation opportunities.

slides.visual_description: Present Workarounds as Opportunity Signals — Identify present workarounds as one source of innovation opportunities.
slides.narration_text: Spot the workaround—extra steps, informal systems, end-runs around the process. Ask what it signals: every workaround marks a gap between design and real need. Then frame the opportunity, because the workaround is the prototype telling you exactly what to build.
slides.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
slides.script_notes: Present Workarounds as Opportunity Signals — Identify present workarounds as one source of innovation opportunities.

slides.visual_description: Future Trends as Opportunity Signals — Identify future trends as one source of innovation opportunities.
slides.narration_text: Read the horizon. Shifts in technology, regulation, demographics, and patient expectations create pressure long before most institutions respond. Leaders who read early solve tomorrow’s problems before they become crises. With those signals in hand, let’s secure the team conditions needed to tell the truth about what’s broken.
slides.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
slides.script_notes: Future Trends as Opportunity Signals — Identify future trends as one source of innovation opportunities.

slides.visual_description: Psychological Safety as a Prerequisite — Understand that teams need psychological safety to report broken systems honestly enough for diagnosis.
slides.narration_text: No diagnostic tool works in a culture of silence. Your team must feel safe saying, “this system is broken,” without fear of blame or consequence. Psychological safety isn’t a soft value—it’s an operational prerequisite for honest reporting and accurate root-cause work. Hold that standard as you step into the leadership capacities that move ideas through a matrixed system.
slides.narrative_arc: From silence about system failure to truthful diagnosis through psychological safety.
slides.script_notes: Psychological Safety as a Prerequisite — Understand that teams need psychological safety to report broken systems honestly enough for diagnosis.

slides.display_title: Leadership Readiness for the Journey Ahead
slides.visual_description: Leadership Readiness for the Journey Ahead — Understand the source-grounded claim that opportunities require a leader with political savvy, communication skills, and leadership identity.
slides.narration_text: An opportunity advances only when a leader can carry it. Build three capacities in parallel: political savvy to create space for change, communication that turns complexity into a compelling narrative, and a leadership identity you truly own—so others can decide to follow you.
slides.narrative_arc: From having an idea to recognizing the need for leadership capacity through emphasis on political savvy, communication, and identity.
slides.script_notes: Leadership Readiness for the Journey Ahead — Understand the source-grounded claim that opportunities require a leader with political savvy, communication skills, and leadership identity.

slides.visual_description: The Idea Needs the Leader — Explain why the source positions leadership capacity as the determinant of whether an innovation opportunity can advance.
slides.narration_text: A brilliant idea goes nowhere without a leader who can carry it—politically, communicatively, and in identity. Leadership capacity is the determinant of whether an opportunity advances. The idea does not succeed on its merits alone; it succeeds because the right leader stepped forward. We’ll build that leader next.
slides.narrative_arc: From having an idea to recognizing the need for leadership capacity through emphasis on political savvy, communication, and identity.
slides.script_notes: The Idea Needs the Leader — Explain why the source positions leadership capacity as the determinant of whether an innovation opportunity can advance.

A.display_title: Module 1 Closure and Transition to Leadership Identity
A.visual_description: Module 1 Closure and Transition to Leadership Identity — Understand the source-grounded summary of Module 1 and the bridge into Module 2, including the shift from innovator mindset to leadership identity.
A.narration_text: Congratulations—your innovator mindset is now set, and the journey deepens. The main message is simple but consequential: we are crossing from how we think about problems to who we must become to lead change. Treat this as a commitment to identity, not a hunt for more tools. As a closing seam, carry forward the discipline you’ve built here and get ready to shape your leadership stance in the next module.
A.narrative_arc: From completion of Module 1 mindset work to readiness for Module 2 leadership identity through a forward-looking synthesis and transition.
A.script_notes: Module 1 Closure and Transition to Leadership Identity — Understand the source-grounded summary of Module 1 and the bridge into Module 2, including the shift from innovator mindset to leadership identity.

A.visual_description: The Intrapreneurial Mandate in Hospitals — Understand that healthcare innovation in this module is framed as intrapreneurship inside existing hospital systems.
A.narration_text: Innovation here is an inside game. You are building change within the hospital—working with politics, budgets, and legacy systems rather than routing around them. When you treat constraints as design inputs, you create momentum that can actually survive governance and scale.
A.narrative_arc: From seeing innovation as a generic idea activity to understanding it as intrapreneurial work inside hospital constraints through explicit framing of politics, budgets, and legacy systems.
A.script_notes: The Intrapreneurial Mandate in Hospitals — Understand that healthcare innovation in this module is framed as intrapreneurship inside existing hospital systems.

A.visual_description: Kind vs. Wicked Environments — Understand the distinction between kind clinical environments and wicked healthcare innovation environments.
A.narration_text: Not all environments reward the same skills. In clinical care, patterns repeat and feedback guides refinement; by contrast, innovation work is ambiguous and the rules keep shifting. Read the environment before you act, or you will apply kind-environment habits to wicked problems and pay for it in rework and resistance.
A.narrative_arc: From assuming clinical problem-solving and innovation follow the same logic to recognizing innovation as a wicked environment through contrast between repetitive medicine and ambiguous system change.
A.script_notes: Kind vs. Wicked Environments — Understand the distinction between kind clinical environments and wicked healthcare innovation environments.

A.visual_description: Why Clinical Medicine Feels Kind — Explain why clinical medicine is described as a kind environment in the source.
A.narration_text: Clinical medicine feels kind because training maps to recognizable patterns, feedback arrives quickly enough to learn, and the rules of practice are stable. That reliability is why repetition builds mastery—and why those instincts are so strong for you.
A.narrative_arc: From assuming clinical problem-solving and innovation follow the same logic to recognizing innovation as a wicked environment through contrast between repetitive medicine and ambiguous system change.
A.script_notes: Why Clinical Medicine Feels Kind — Explain why clinical medicine is described as a kind environment in the source.

A.visual_description: Why Innovation Work Becomes Wicked — Explain why healthcare innovation is described as wicked, ambiguous, and variable.
A.narration_text: Innovation work becomes wicked when the goal posts are unclear, feedback is delayed or misleading, and policies or priorities shift mid-journey. That volatility isn’t failure—it’s the terrain. Closing the contrast, hold this thought as we pivot: if the work is wicked, your habits must flex. Next, we’ll make that flexibility concrete.
A.narrative_arc: From assuming clinical problem-solving and innovation follow the same logic to recognizing innovation as a wicked environment through contrast between repetitive medicine and ambiguous system change.
A.script_notes: Why Innovation Work Becomes Wicked — Explain why healthcare innovation is described as wicked, ambiguous, and variable.

A.visual_description: Functional Flexibility — Understand that clinical leaders must adapt beyond rigid specialty tools and borrow from other disciplines.
A.narration_text: Functional flexibility is your edge in wicked conditions. Borrow frameworks, language, and tools from operations, design, business, and behavioral science when the situation calls for it. Rigid specialty thinking that serves you at the bedside becomes a liability in system change.
A.narrative_arc: From relying only on specialty-specific habits to embracing cross-functional leadership tools through the expectation of disciplined borrowing.
A.script_notes: Functional Flexibility — Understand that clinical leaders must adapt beyond rigid specialty tools and borrow from other disciplines.

A.visual_description: Clinical Diagnosis vs. Systemic Diagnosis — Understand the analogy between clinical diagnosis and operational diagnosis before selecting solutions.
A.narration_text: Lead innovation with the same diagnostic discipline you trust in clinical care: observe, form hypotheses, confirm, then intervene. One path assesses symptoms to find a cause; the other audits systems to surface a root cause. The shared method is the point—understand before you act.
A.narrative_arc: From solution-first thinking to disciplined root-cause diagnosis through analogy with clinical diagnostic practice.
A.script_notes: Clinical Diagnosis vs. Systemic Diagnosis — Understand the analogy between clinical diagnosis and operational diagnosis before selecting solutions.

A.visual_description: Do Not Prescribe Before Diagnosing — Explain the clinical half of the analogy that anchors the leadership diagnostic mindset.
A.narration_text: Clinically, you never prescribe before assessing. You gather data, build a differential, and test hypotheses. That same rigor—discipline before remedy—is the anchor for your leadership choices.
A.narrative_arc: From solution-first thinking to disciplined root-cause diagnosis through analogy with clinical diagnostic practice.
A.script_notes: Do Not Prescribe Before Diagnosing — Explain the clinical half of the analogy that anchors the leadership diagnostic mindset.

A.display_title: Do Not Buy or Build Before Diagnosing the Root Cause
A.visual_description: Do Not Buy or Build Before Diagnosing the Root Cause — Apply the diagnostic analogy to innovation decisions inside operational systems.
A.narration_text: Operationally, buying or building on first impression is the parallel mistake. The disciplined move is to investigate the system, confirm the root cause, and only then design the solution. Stitching the analogy closed, we’ll now guard against a second trap: falling in love with a solution instead of the problem.
A.narrative_arc: From solution-first thinking to disciplined root-cause diagnosis through analogy with clinical diagnostic practice.
A.script_notes: Do Not Buy or Build Before Diagnosing the Root Cause — Apply the diagnostic analogy to innovation decisions inside operational systems.

A.display_title: Falling in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution
A.visual_description: Falling in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution — Understand that innovators fail when they become attached to solutions instead of accurately defining the problem.
A.narration_text: The most common failure in innovation is attachment to a favorite solution before the problem is truly understood. When you’re attached, you reshape the problem to fit your idea. Discipline means staying curious about the problem, especially when that curiosity feels uncomfortable.
A.narrative_arc: From solution attachment to disciplined problem focus through a direct warning about innovation failure.
A.script_notes: Falling in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution — Understand that innovators fail when they become attached to solutions instead of accurately defining the problem.

A.visual_description: Symptom vs. Root Cause — Distinguish between visible pain points and underlying system failure.
A.narration_text: Visible pain points matter, but they’re rarely the source. Treating symptoms without surfacing underlying causes buys temporary relief and guarantees recurrence. A system that keeps producing the same complaint hasn’t been diagnosed—it’s only been managed.
A.narrative_arc: From reacting to visible pain to distinguishing hidden system failure through symptom-versus-root-cause analysis.
A.script_notes: Symptom vs. Root Cause — Distinguish between visible pain points and underlying system failure.

A.display_title: What Looks Broken vs. What Actually Is Broken
A.visual_description: What Looks Broken vs. What Actually Is Broken — Explain the operational difference between visible symptoms and underlying causes.
A.narration_text: What looks broken—complaints, delays, frustration—is the surface presentation. What’s actually broken lives in structure: incentives, accountability, process design. Close the gap by naming the structure, not just the symptom. With that lens in place, we can aim for leverage next.
A.narrative_arc: From reacting to visible pain to distinguishing hidden system failure through symptom-versus-root-cause analysis.
A.script_notes: What Looks Broken vs. What Actually Is Broken — Explain the operational difference between visible symptoms and underlying causes.

A.visual_description: The Lead Domino — Understand that solving the true root cause can eliminate multiple downstream symptoms.
A.narration_text: Leverage comes from finding the lead domino—the structural fix that, once addressed, collapses a chain of visible failures without separate projects for each symptom. Hunt for the intervention that makes many other problems irrelevant.
A.narrative_arc: From isolated symptom treatment to leverage-based system change through the idea of the lead domino.
A.script_notes: The Lead Domino — Understand that solving the true root cause can eliminate multiple downstream symptoms.

A.visual_description: The 5 Whys Framework — Understand the 5 Whys as the module's primary operational tool for surfacing root causes.
A.narration_text: Use the Five Whys to move past assumptions and into structure. First, ask why the observed problem happens. Then ask why again, letting each answer become the next question. Keep going until your answer points to something you can actually change.
A.narrative_arc: From vague operational frustration to a usable root-cause method through repeated why-questioning.
A.script_notes: The 5 Whys Framework — Understand the 5 Whys as the module's primary operational tool for surfacing root causes.

A.visual_description: Why the 5 Whys Matters — Explain why the 5 Whys is central to operational diagnosis in this module.
A.narration_text: Most hospital decisions happen at the symptom level, which is why problems recur. The Five Whys interrupts that cycle—simple, no tech required, and it surfaces what metrics alone miss. It also builds shared understanding by forcing reflection before action.
A.narrative_arc: From vague operational frustration to a usable root-cause method through repeated why-questioning.
A.script_notes: Why the 5 Whys Matters — Explain why the 5 Whys is central to operational diagnosis in this module.

A.display_title: Asking Why Until a Root Cause Emerges
A.visual_description: Asking Why Until a Root Cause Emerges — Describe the basic action of the 5 Whys framework as stated in the source.
A.narration_text: State the observed problem clearly—only what you can see and measure. Ask why it’s happening, then ask why again, resisting the urge to stop early. Stop when action becomes possible—when the answer points to something your team can actually change. With that root in hand, we can widen our scan for opportunities.
A.narrative_arc: From vague operational frustration to a usable root-cause method through repeated why-questioning.
A.script_notes: Asking Why Until a Root Cause Emerges — Describe the basic action of the 5 Whys framework as stated in the source.

A.visual_description: The Opportunity Radar — Understand that innovation opportunities are generated by systematically auditing frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
A.narration_text: Great ideas rarely introduce themselves. Build an opportunity radar by auditing three domains: past frustrations, present workarounds, and future trends. When you scan systematically, you stop waiting for inspiration and start finding leverage.
A.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
A.script_notes: The Opportunity Radar — Understand that innovation opportunities are generated by systematically auditing frustrations, workarounds, and trends.

A.visual_description: Past Frustrations as Opportunity Signals — Identify past frustrations as one source of innovation opportunities.
A.narration_text: Past frustrations are gold. They mark real pain the system normalized rather than solved. Revisit what was dismissed or tolerated—through an innovator’s lens, those moments often reveal opportunities hiding in plain sight.
A.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
A.script_notes: Past Frustrations as Opportunity Signals — Identify past frustrations as one source of innovation opportunities.

A.visual_description: Present Workarounds as Opportunity Signals — Identify present workarounds as one source of innovation opportunities.
A.narration_text: Spot the workaround—extra steps, informal systems, end-runs around the process. Ask what it signals: every workaround marks a gap between design and real need. Then frame the opportunity, because the workaround is the prototype telling you exactly what to build.
A.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
A.script_notes: Present Workarounds as Opportunity Signals — Identify present workarounds as one source of innovation opportunities.

A.visual_description: Future Trends as Opportunity Signals — Identify future trends as one source of innovation opportunities.
A.narration_text: Read the horizon. Shifts in technology, regulation, demographics, and patient expectations create pressure long before most institutions respond. Leaders who read early solve tomorrow’s problems before they become crises. With those signals in hand, let’s secure the team conditions needed to tell the truth about what’s broken.
A.narrative_arc: From waiting passively for ideas to building a systematic scan for opportunities through an audit of frustrations, workarounds, and trends.
A.script_notes: Future Trends as Opportunity Signals — Identify future trends as one source of innovation opportunities.

A.visual_description: Psychological Safety as a Prerequisite — Understand that teams need psychological safety to report broken systems honestly enough for diagnosis.
A.narration_text: No diagnostic tool works in a culture of silence. Your team must feel safe saying, “this system is broken,” without fear of blame or consequence. Psychological safety isn’t a soft value—it’s an operational prerequisite for honest reporting and accurate root-cause work. Hold that standard as you step into the leadership capacities that move ideas through a matrixed system.
A.narrative_arc: From silence about system failure to truthful diagnosis through psychological safety.
A.script_notes: Psychological Safety as a Prerequisite — Understand that teams need psychological safety to report broken systems honestly enough for diagnosis.

A.display_title: Leadership Readiness for the Journey Ahead
A.visual_description: Leadership Readiness for the Journey Ahead — Understand the source-grounded claim that opportunities require a leader with political savvy, communication skills, and leadership identity.
A.narration_text: An opportunity advances only when a leader can carry it. Build three capacities in parallel: political savvy to create space for change, communication that turns complexity into a compelling narrative, and a leadership identity you truly own—so others can decide to follow you.
A.narrative_arc: From having an idea to recognizing the need for leadership capacity through emphasis on political savvy, communication, and identity.
A.script_notes: Leadership Readiness for the Journey Ahead — Understand the source-grounded claim that opportunities require a leader with political savvy, communication skills, and leadership identity.

A.visual_description: The Idea Needs the Leader — Explain why the source positions leadership capacity as the determinant of whether an innovation opportunity can advance.
A.narration_text: A brilliant idea goes nowhere without a leader who can carry it—politically, communicatively, and in identity. Leadership capacity is the determinant of whether an opportunity advances. The idea does not succeed on its merits alone; it succeeds because the right leader stepped forward. We’ll build that leader next.
A.narrative_arc: From having an idea to recognizing the need for leadership capacity through emphasis on political savvy, communication, and identity.
A.script_notes: The Idea Needs the Leader — Explain why the source positions leadership capacity as the determinant of whether an innovation opportunity can advance.
